## Generalized Linear Models


Generalized Linear Models (GLM) are a way of extending the Linear Modeling framework to situations where the outcome is not continuous.

::: fragment
Every GLM has three components:

1. A specific [probability distribution]{.yellow} (Y) for the outcome variable. Such as: normal, binomial, poisson, gamma etc.

2. A systematic component ($\eta$) that is a linear function of the independent variables (this looks like a linear model $\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \beta_2X_2...$)

3. A link function $g$ that transforms the linear component into the expected value on the outcome scale (and that can be inverted to transform the outcome back to the linear scale.)

:::

## Notation note

We'll use some matrix notation here just to make things a bit more readable. Just note that this:

$$
X'\beta
$$

Is the same thing as the linear model we've been writing:

$$
\beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \beta_2X_2... = 
$$



## Generalized Linear Models: dichotomous outcomes

We want to use a line to model $y= X'\beta$, but a linear model doesn't quite work here.

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Probabilities should be bounded between 0 and 1, but a line can go from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$

- In practice, we typically see "diminishing returns" for dichotomous outcomes: changing x has a bigger effect when the probability of y=1 is close to .5 compared to when it's close to .99.



:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}

set.seed(123)


# 1. Define sample size and parameters
n <- 100
beta_0 <- -1.0   # Intercept
beta_1 <- 0.7    # Slope for predictor x
# 2. Generate a random predictor variable (e.g., normal or uniform)
x <- runif(n, min=-10, max=10)
# 3. Calculate log-odds (logit of probabilities)
log_odds <- beta_0 + beta_1 * x
# 4. Convert log-odds to probabilities using the inverse-logit (sigmoid) function
p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-log_odds))
# 5. Generate binary response variable (0 or 1) using a binomial distribution
y <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = p)

            newdata =data.frame(x=min(x), max(x), by=.1)
# Combine into a data frame
sim_data <- data.frame(x = x, log_odds = log_odds, prob = p, y = y)

ggplot(data=sim_data,aes(x=x, y=y))+ 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method='lm', se=FALSE)


```
:::
:::::


## Generalized Linear Models: dichotomous outcomes


So, we need a function that transforms a continuous input into values that are bounded between 0 and 1 and that has a steeper slope towards the center compared to the ends.


## Generalized Linear Models: dichotomous outcomes


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- One option is to use a logit link function. This amounts to modeling $\log{\frac{p}{1-p}} = \beta ' X $. This amounts to modeling the logged odds of y=1. 

- This gives us the [logit model]{.yellow}.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
invlogit<-function(x){
  ret<-1/(1+exp(-x))
  return(ret)
}

ggplot() +
  xlim(-10, 10) +
  geom_function(fun = invlogit, color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  xlab("logged odds") +
  ylab("probability")

```
:::
:::::




## Generalized Linear Models: dichotomous outcomes


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Another option is to use the probit function $\Phi^{-1}(XB)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (the same integral math that turns a z-score into a probability under the normal distribution)

- This gives us the [probit model]{.yellow}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
invprobit<-function(x){
  x<-pnorm(x)
}

ggplot() +
  xlim(-10, 10) +
  geom_function(fun = invprobit, color = "red", linewidth = 1,lty=2) +
  xlab("probit") +
  ylab("probability")

```
:::
:::::



## Logit and probit



::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Both the [logit]{.yellow} and [probit]{.yellow} models will give us a result that is bounded between 0 and 1.

- The logit model has slightly "fatter tails", but, in practice, the results tend to be substantively very similar.

- Today, logit models are more common because they have a slightly more intuitive interpretation than probit models.


:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{ojs}
//| panel: sidebar
viewof beta0 = Inputs.range([-5, 5], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: html`<b>Intercept (β₀)</b>`})
viewof beta1 = Inputs.range([0.1, 5], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: html`<b>Slope (β₁)</b>`})
```

```{ojs}
// 1. Import jStat for a robust, natively tested standard normal CDF implementation
jStat = require("jstat@1.9.6")

// 2. Generate the domain grid
xValues = d3.range(-6, 6.01, 0.05)

// 3. Map the clean, verified data structure
chartData = xValues.flatMap(x => {
  const linearPredictor = beta0 + beta1 * x;
  
  // Logit (Logistic Link)
  const pLogit = 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-linearPredictor));
  
  // Probit (Standard Normal Cumulative Distribution) using jStat
  // Parameters for jStat.normal.cdf are: (x, mean, stdDev)
  const pProbit = jStat.normal.cdf(linearPredictor, 0, 1);
  
  return [
    { x: x, probability: pLogit, model: "Logit (Logistic CDF)" },
    { x: x, probability: pProbit, model: "Probit (Normal CDF)" }
  ];
})
```

```{ojs}
// 4. Render the chart with structural axis lines, ticks, and dynamic changeover indicators
Plot.plot({
  title: `Probability Curves for Linear Predictor: z = ${beta0.toFixed(1)} + ${beta1.toFixed(1)} * X`,
  subtitle: "Corrected Probit implementation using jStat",
  grid: true,
  x: { domain: [-6, 6], label: "Explanatory Variable (X)" },
  y: { domain:, label: "Predicted Probability P(Y=1)" },
  color: {
    domain: ["Logit (Logistic CDF)", "Probit (Normal CDF)"],
    range: ["#2c7bb6", "#d7191c"],
    legend: true
  },
  marks: [
    // 1. Structural axis lines and tick marks
    Plot.axisX({anchor: "bottom", tickSize: 6, stroke: "#333"}),
    Plot.axisY({anchor: "left", tickSize: 6, stroke: "#333"}),

    // 2. Horizontal baseline visual anchor at y = 0.5
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], { stroke: "#aaa", strokeDasharray: "4,4" }),
    
    // 3. DYNAMIC CHANGEOVER POINT (Vertical Red Dashed Line)
    // Formula: x = -beta0 / beta1 when linear predictor equals 0
    Plot.ruleX([-beta0 / beta1], {
      stroke: "#d7191c",
      strokeDasharray: "5,5",
      strokeWidth: 1.5
    }),

    // 4. Text label tracking the changeover point coordinate
    Plot.text([-beta0 / beta1], {
      y: 0.55, 
      text: d => `X = ${d.toFixed(2)}`,
      textAnchor: "start",
      dx: 8,
      fill: "#d7191c",
      fontWeight: "bold"
    }),
    
    // 5. Continuous probability curves
    Plot.line(chartData, {
      x: "x",
      y: "probability",
      stroke: "model",
      strokeWidth: 2.5
    })
  ]
})
```

  xlim(-10, 10) +
  geom_function(fun = invprobit, color = "blue", linewidth = 1,) +

## Generalized Linear Models: dichotomous outcomes

So, now we've got everything we need for a generalized linear model:

1. Our outcome has a binomial distribution where everything is a 1 or a 0.

2. We have a systematic component that can be defined with a linear model $\eta= X'B$

3. We have a function (such as logit) that can map $\eta$ onto the response scale.

## Fitting GLMs


In a linear model, we can identify the line of best fit by minimizing the sum of squared residuals, but we don't really have a direct analog for this when we've transformed the outcome like this.

So how do I know whether one model is better than any other?



```{r}
set.seed(123)


# 1. Define sample size and parameters
n <- 100
beta_0 <- -1.0   # Intercept
beta_1 <- 0.7    # Slope for predictor x
# 2. Generate a random predictor variable (e.g., normal or uniform)
x <- runif(n, min=-10, max=10)
# 3. Calculate log-odds (logit of probabilities)
log_odds <- beta_0 + beta_1 * x
# 4. Convert log-odds to probabilities using the inverse-logit (sigmoid) function
p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-log_odds))
# 5. Generate binary response variable (0 or 1) using a binomial distribution
y <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = p)

            newdata =data.frame(x=min(x), max(x), by=.1)
# Combine into a data frame
sim_data <- data.frame(x = x, log_odds = log_odds, prob = p, y = y)

ggplot(data=sim_data,aes(x=x, y=y))+ 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method='glm',
              method.args = list(family = "binomial"), 
              se=FALSE)


```


## Maximum Likelihood Estimation

- Rather than minimizing the sum of squared errors, most generalized linear models will find the best fit using [Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)]{.yellow}

- In MLE, we find the set of parameter values (typically denoted using the symbol $\theta$) that are *most likely* to have generated the data we see.

- We'll look at a simple application to get a sense of how this works.



## MLE of a proportion


- Imagine a survey of 100 randomly selected adults finds that about 26% believe in bigfoot 

- What is the population probability of Bigfoot belief ($\theta$) that is [most likely]{.yellow} to have generated this result?


## MLE of a proportion

$\theta$ *could* be any number $>0$  and $<1$. It's *possible* to get a sample where 26% believe in Bigfoot even if the population percent is 40%:

```{r}
#| cache: true
#| fig-height: 3
set.seed(1000)

df<-data.frame(x=rbinom(1e6, 100, .40))

ggplot(df, aes(x=x)) + geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline(xintercept=26, lty=2, color='red') +
  labs(title = "1 million simulated samples",
       subtitle = "n = 100; θ = .40",
     xlab="Number of sampled respondents who believe in Bigfoot")

```

::: fragment

You can probably already guess that the correct answer here is $\theta = .26$, but we want a way to *systematically* pick the best value of $\theta$ for more complicated problems.

:::

## MLE of a proportion


Since "belief in Bigfoot" is a simple yes/no question, then we can model a single response using the Bernoulli Probability Mass Function:

$$
\begin{align*}
P(y_i=1|\theta) = \theta^{y_i}(1-\theta)^{1-y_i}\\
\theta = \text{probability that y is 1}\\
y_i = \text{a single response to the question}
\end{align*}
$$


. . .


So, if $y_i=1$ and $\theta = .20$

$$
P(1|.20) = .20^{1}(.75)^{0} = .20
$$


. . .


If $y_i=0$ and $\theta = .20$ 

$$
P(0|.20) = .20^{0}(.80)^{1} = .80
$$

## MLE of a proportion

Assuming that the observations are all independent and identically distributed, we can calculate the *likelihood* of the entire sample by simply multiplying together all the individual probabilities from each of the 100 observations:

$$
L(y|\theta) =  \prod^n_{i=1} \theta^{y_i}(1-\theta)^{1-y_i} = \theta^{\sum{y_i}}(1-\theta)^{n-\sum{y_i}}
$$


::: fragment

However, we run into a bit of a computational problem here because the likelihood gets very small very quickly:

```{r}
#| echo: true

.25 * .25 * .75 * .25 * .25 * .25 * .75 * .25 # ... and so on

```

:::

::: fragment 

Using a logarithm gets around this problem by turning the tiny fractions into large negative numbers, and allowing us to use addition rather than multiplication:

```{r}
#| echo: true
log(.25) + log(.25) + log(.75) + log(.25) + log(.25) + log(.25) + log(.75)  + log(.25)

```

:::

::: fragment



```{r}
#| echo: true

exp(-8.89313)

```

:::

## MLE of a proportion

$$
\theta^{\sum{y_i}}(1-\theta)^{n-\sum{y_i}}
$$


::: fragment


Taking the log here turns the multiplication into addition, and the exponentiation into multiplication:

$$
\log L(y|\theta) = (\sum^n_{i=1}y_i) \log(\theta) + (n-\sum^n_{i=1}{y_i}) \log(1-\theta)
$$

:::

## MLE of a proportion

So now we have a function we can use to distinguish good guesses at $\theta$ from bad guesses: we just want to find a parameter that maximizes this function:

$$
\log L(y|\theta) = (\sum^n_{i=1}y_i) \log(\theta) + (n-\sum^n_{i=1}{y_i}) \log(1-\theta)
$$


```{r}
#| echo: true
# 100 responses with p = .26
y<-rep(c(0, 1), c(74, 26))
ll_prop<-function(y, theta){
  n<-length(y)
  sumy<-sum(y)
  ll<-sumy * log(theta) + (n-sumy) * log(1-theta)
  return(ll)
}


ll_prop(y, .5)
ll_prop(y, .4)
ll_prop(y, .8)

```


## MLE of a proportion

Again, we could probably just eyeball this, but to find it mathematically we would need to do a bit of calculus:

```{r}
curve(ll_prop(y=y, theta=x), from = .01, to = .99, 
      xname ='x',
      xlab ='Theta',
      ylab  ="log likelihood",
      main = "Plot if logged likelihoods for different values of theta", 
      col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(v = .26, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = "dashed")


```


## MLE of a proportion

The maximum is the point where the derivative (slope) of this line with respect to $\theta$ is 0 (and where the second derivative of this line is negative)



```{r}
# 1. Define the data (Number of successes 'x' and total trials 'n')
x <- 26
n <- 100
mle <- x / n  # The Maximum Likelihood Estimate (0.26)

# 2. Define a sequence of possible proportion values (p) 
# We slightly exclude exact 0 and 1 to prevent log(0) or division by zero errors
p <- seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 500)

# 3. Calculate Log-Likelihood and its Derivative (Score function)
# Log-likelihood: l(p) = x*log(p) + (n-x)*log(1-p)
log_likelihood <- x * log(p) + (n - x) * log(1 - p)

# Derivative: dl/dp = x/p - (n-x)/(1-p)
derivative <- (x / p) - ((n - x) / (1 - p))

# 4. Set up a side-by-side plotting layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# --- Plot 1: Log-Likelihood ---
plot(p, log_likelihood, type = "l", col = "blue", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "θ", ylab = "Log-Likelihood l(θ)",
     main = "Log-Likelihood of a Proportion")

# Add a vertical dashed line at the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE)
abline(v = mle, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
text(mle, min(log_likelihood)+.8, labels = paste("MLE =", mle), pos = 4, col = "red")

# --- Plot 2: Derivative of Log-Likelihood (Score Function) ---
plot(p, derivative, type = "l", col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "θ", ylab = "dl / dθ",
     main = "Derivative of Log-Likelihood")

# Add a horizontal line at 0 (where derivative equals zero)
abline(h = 0, col = "black", lty = 1)
# Add a vertical dashed line at the root (MLE)
abline(v = mle, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)

# Reset plotting parameters back to default
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

```

## MLE of a proportion

The maximum is the point where the derivative (slope) of this line with respect to $\theta$ is 0 (and where the second derivative of this line is negative)

$$
\log L(y|\theta) = (\sum^n_{i=1}y_i) \log(\theta) + (n-\sum^n_{i=1}{y_i}) \log(1-\theta)
$$

## MLE of a proportion

Simplifying the notation a bit...

$$
\begin{align*}
&Y \log(\theta) + (n-Y) \log(1-\theta)\\
\end{align*}
$$

where $Y = \sum^n_{i=1}{y_i}$

::: fragment


Applying the [chain rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_rule)

$$
Y \frac{1}{\theta} +  (n-Y) \frac{-1}{1-\theta}
$$

:::

::: fragment

And simplifying...

$$
\frac{d}{d\theta} = \frac{Y}{\theta} +  \frac{(n-Y) }{1-\theta}
$$


:::

## MLE of a proportion


Now we can set it to zero and solve algebraically for $\theta$

$$
0 = \frac{Y}{\theta} +  \frac{(n-Y) }{1-\theta}
$$

. . .


$$
\begin{align}
\frac{Y}{\theta} =  \frac{(n-Y) }{1-\theta}  && \text{Adding } \frac{(n-Y) }{1-\theta} \text{ to both sides} \\
Y(1-\theta) =(n-Y)\theta   && \text{cross multiplying by } \theta(1-\theta)\\ 
Y-Y\theta  = n\theta - Y\theta && \text{Expanding}\\
Y = n\theta  && \text{Cancelling } -Y\theta\\ 
\theta = \frac{Y}{n} && \text{Solving for } \theta
\end{align}
$$


## MLE of a proportion

What is the population probability of Bigfoot belief ($\theta$) that is [most likely]{.yellow} to have generated a sample with 26% Bigfoot believers?

. . .

The estimate of $\theta$ that maximizes the likelihood of observing our data is just the sample proportion: .26!

$$
\begin{align*}
\hat{\theta} = \frac{Y}{n}  \\
\end{align*}
$$

### Key points

The answer here was kind of obvious to begin with, but Maximum Likelihood Estimation is useful because it gives us a flexible way to judge models where we don't have an easy metric like the sum of squared errors.

. . .

For instance, we could estimate the conditional probability of belief in Bigfoot as a function of some predictors ($X$)


$$
L(y|\beta, X) =  \prod^n_{i=1} (\text{logit}^{-1} X_i\beta)^{y_i}(1-\text{logit}^{-1} X_i\beta)^{1-y_i}
$$


::: fragment

We've definitely made the problem here more complex, but
